# Revelation 22: verse-by-verse research notes

**Gaps to know about.** I ran out of searches before I could check several sources, so these notes leave out:
- Wesley's own notes on most verses (I only have his note on v. 16).
- NET Bible notes beyond one word note on v. 16.
- Most Orthodox and Catholic comment. The only Catholic material I found was on vv. 18–19.
- Bible Odyssey.
- Anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.

Enduring Word only came through as far as v. 10. My notes on Ellicott for vv. 6–15 come from search-result excerpts of his chapter page.

---

**v. 1**
- Ellicott says the river stands for life in its "gladness, purity, activity, and fulness". It recalls the river in Eden. The river is full of water, and that water is the emblem of life: it is the beautiful symbol of life in its gladness, purity, activity, and fulness. The garden of Eden (Genesis 2:10) had its river. He also says the word "pure" should be dropped because the best manuscripts don't have it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Guzik draws on Old Testament prophets who pictured a river as plenty and peace (Isaiah 48, Zechariah 14, Ezekiel 47). Through the Old Testament, prophets used the picture of a river as a powerful expression of richness, provision, and peace (Isaiah 48:18, Zechariah 14:8, Ezekiel 47:1-9). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-22/
- Precept Austin (Tony Garland, dispensational) treats it as a real river that also pictures the Holy Spirit. Although this is a literal river in the eternal state, it also typifies the Holy Spirit Who cleanses and gives life to those who trust Christ in this age. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-22-commentary
- Gill (Baptist, Calvinist) is different. He says the river means God's everlasting love, which flows out in election, redemption, calling and justification. rather, therefore, by this river is meant the everlasting love of God https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-1.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the river is described flowing out but never reaching a mouth. eternity is the ocean in which this river is lost. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik sees Eden's tree of life given back. He quotes Walvoord, who pictures one large tree spanning the river, and Spurgeon, who pictures rows of trees on both banks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-22/
- On "healing", Guzik follows Walvoord: the Greek word can mean "health-giving". It's a little hard to picture this heavenly landscaping. John may be describing a large street with a river flowing down the middle, and a large tree – or series of trees – that grows with roots on either side of the river. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-22/
- Ellicott: twelve kinds of fruit show variety held together in unity, yet there is still one tree of life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Gill says the tree is Christ himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-2.htm
- Precept Austin equates access to the tree with salvation. It also notes a debated suggestion that the "nations" might be people still in natural bodies. Evidently, access to the tree of life is one and the same as salvation https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-22-commentary

**v. 3**
- Ellicott renders it "every accursed thing" will be gone. God's presence and rule replace the hold evil has had over a groaning creation. All accursed things are removed, and with them passes the curse. The blessing of God's presence, and the blessing of God's rule take the place of the ascendancy of evil over the groaning creation (Romans 8:22). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Ellicott on "serve": the Greek word is the one used for temple service. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Guzik (premillennial) says parts of the curse remain during the Millennium and are only removed for good here. He quotes Leon Morris that heaven is not a place of idle leisure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-22/

**v. 4**
- Ellicott links seeing God's face with 1 Corinthians 13:12 and 1 John 3:2. The name stands for what God is in holiness and righteousness, purity and love. The name on the forehead indicates their resemblance to their Master. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Guzik cites Spurgeon: this means both literally seeing Jesus with risen eyes and understanding him far more deeply. Spurgeon calls it "the heaven of heaven". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-22/

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: no artificial light is needed. Those once made kings and priests (Revelation 1:6) now reign. No artificial light is needed, since He who is Light is their light. Those who were children of light now dwell in the light of God's countenance https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Gill: God gives light directly, without using means and ordinances. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-5.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: "faithful and true" covers the whole book. "The God of the spirits of the prophets" means the God who moved the prophets (2 Peter 1:21). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Precept Austin argues strongly for a literal-future reading: the book is not an allegory from which readers can extract hidden meanings of their own concoction. It is an accurate description of events and persons yet to come. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-22-commentary

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: the blessing comes from keeping the words, not from reading, wondering or talking about them. It is not in reading, or wondering, or talking, but in keeping, that the blessing comes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- How "soon" should be read is a real dividing line between schools of interpretation:
  - Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan that "quickly" could be rendered "suddenly". He quotes Mounce that the "time has always been at hand" between the cross and Christ's return. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-22/
  - Garland (dispensational) reads "soon" as imminence: no conditions remain before Christ could return. He warns that partial preterism tends to slide into full preterism, which he calls heterodox. the solution is found in understanding "soon" as an indication from God's perspective that no more preconditions remain before Christ could return. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-22-commentary

**vv. 8–9**
- Ellicott: John adds his own testimony as the one who "hears and sees". The worship twice offered and twice refused teaches that giving inflated honour to any creature "inverts God's order". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Guzik: only God may be worshipped, whereas Jesus does receive worship (Hebrews 1:6). He adds that visions are no guarantee of sound doctrine. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-22/
- Protestant use against Catholic practice:
  - Guzik quotes Seiss arguing from this verse against praying to the Virgin Mary. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-22/
  - Matthew Henry calls it another testimony against idolatrous worship of saints and angels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-19.htm
  - I didn't find a Catholic response on the allowed sites.

**v. 10**
- Ellicott contrasts this with Daniel, who was told to seal his book. The angel, in contrast to the injunctions given to Daniel (Daniel 12:9-13), bids the prophet "Seal not the words of the prophecy" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Barnes: the book was meant to comfort a persecuted church right away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-10.htm
- Gill draws a Protestant point: the Scriptures in general are not to be locked up, and concealed from the common people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-10.htm

**v. 11**
Commentators read this verse three different ways:
- **Character becomes fixed.** Barnes says the person's state will be settled forever. their condition will be fixed, and that they will remain in this state of pollution forever. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-11.htm
- **Ironic.** The Pulpit Commentary reads it as irony, like Ezekiel 3:27. These words seem to be used ironically, as was sometimes the case with the prophets https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-11.htm
- **A moral law.** Ellicott sees the law by which acts ripen into habits and habits shape destiny. men by continuing in sin (Revelation 22:11) are inviting against themselves the law by which act ripens to habit, and habit makes character, and character forms destiny. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Precept Austin applies Ezekiel's pattern: the messenger's job is to deliver the message faithfully, not to own the results. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-22-commentary

**v. 12**
- Ellicott hears Isaiah 40:10 and Paul's "whatsoever a man soweth" (Galatians 6:7). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Precept Austin: Christians should examine their motives in light of the coming reward. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_47-8

**v. 13**
- Ellicott ties the titles to vv. 11–12. Those caught by the moral consequences of their sin find refuge in the eternal God himself. the refuge from the eternal laws which we invoke against ourselves by our sin is to be found in the Eternal God https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm

**v. 14**
There is a manuscript difference here: the older manuscripts read "wash their robes", while the Received Text (behind the KJV) reads "do his commandments".
- Ellicott: the received reading The reading of two of the best MSS. is, "Blessed are they that wash their robes.". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Precept Austin notes the same variant. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-22-commentary
- Matthew Henry, using the "commandments" reading: Never let us think that a dead or disobedient faith will save us, because only those who do his commandments are called blessed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-19.htm

**v. 15**
- Ellicott: dogs were unclean animals, so they are pictured outside the city. The dog, moreover, was an unclean animal; dogs, therefore, are represented as outside the city, because nothing unclean is allowed to enter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/22.htm
- Pulpit: "the dogs" are the "filthy" of v. 11, a proverbial term in the East for the most degraded. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-15.htm

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: Jesus is David's Lord and David's Son, and the star that leads in everlasting day. He is David's Lord and David's Son, possessing David's throne (Matthew 22:42-45; Luke 1:32); He is the bright star which leads up the dawn of everlasting day https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-16.htm
- Wesley (Methodist): Jesus is the root of David as God and his offspring as man. The morning star ends the night of ignorance, sin, and sorrow, and usher in an eternal day of light, purity, and joy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/22-16.html
- Got Questions: the "morning star" title also contrasts with Satan, the fallen star. https://www.gotquestions.org/bright-morning-star.html
- NET Bible note: the Greek lexicon BDAG identifies the morning star as Venus. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=rev&chapter=22&verse=16

**v. 17**
- Guzik stresses how open the invitation is. It requires no grasp of doctrine, no perfect repentance and no worthiness, only desire. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-22/
- Alford reads the verse as John's reply to Christ's words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/alford/revelation/22.htm
- How Calvinist and Arminian writers frame the invitation:
  - Clarke (Methodist) takes it as proof of universal atonement: No soul is excluded: Jesus died for every man; every man may be saved. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/revelation-22.html
  - A Biblical Illustrator sermon, in Reformed covenant language, roots the fountain in the deep foundations of God's decrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/revelation-22.html

**v. 18**
- Most commentators compare it with Deuteronomy 4:2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-18.htm
- Gill: honest exposition of Scripture is not "adding". Twisting it, or putting unwritten traditions on a level with it, is. He sees the canon closed here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-18.htm
- Does it cover the whole Bible? Protestants disagree among themselves:
  - Barnes says it refers to the book of Revelation only - for at that time the books that now constitute what we call the Bible were not collected into a single volume. This passage, therefore, should not be adduced as referring to the whole of the sacred Scriptures. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-18.htm
  - Coffman (Restoration Movement) says the opposite: "book of this prophecy" means the whole Bible. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/22-18.html
  - Chafer, quoted by Precept Austin, says the closing of the New Testament canon is "at least intimated". https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-22-commentary
- Catholic reading: the verse forbids tampering with Revelation's own text. It does not prove sola scriptura or rule out God's word outside the Bible. But John, the author of Revelation, was just prohibiting the addition of words to the visions he received. He was not denying that the word of God exists outside the Bible https://shop.catholic.com/blog/the-unbiblical-idea-of-sola-scriptura-/
- Karlo Broussard (Catholic) turns the usual Protestant charge around. If the verse meant the whole canon, Protestants would be guilty of "taking away" the deuterocanonical books. https://shop.catholic.com/blog/dont-add-to-gods-word/

**v. 19**
- Textual note: the best manuscripts read "tree of life", not "book of life". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-19.htm
- Can a true believer lose their share? I found two Calvinist-leaning answers (Gill and Barnes). I could not retrieve a Methodist voice on this verse.
  - Gill (Baptist, Calvinist): the book of life means eternal election, and everyone written in it will certainly be saved. Those warned here only *seemed* to have a part. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-19.htm
  - Barnes (Presbyterian) takes the same direction: the meaning is not that his name had been written in that book, but that he would take away the part which he might have had, or which he professed to have. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-19.htm

**v. 20**
- Precept Austin: from God's timeless point of view the delay is short. From ours, it shows God's grace and mercy. The lengthy delay from our perspective is a great testimony to the grace and mercy of God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-22-commentary

**v. 21**
- Ellicott notes that manuscripts differ between "with all" and "with the saints". Either way, grace is the last word. In any case, it is the grace or free pardon of the Lord Jesus which is the last word left in our ears. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-21.htm
- Pulpit: the book closes the way the message began in Revelation 1:4. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/22-21.htm
